extracted.intended_audience: journalists, newsroom leaders, journalism students, and the general public interested in journalism organizations
extracted.subtask_description: Summarizes the American Society of News Editors' organizational standards, initiatives, membership rules, measurement practices, awards categories, and program focus areas used to evaluate or guide journalistic organizations and practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Code of ethics
rubrics_metrics.description: Founders decided to 'develop a constitution and a code of ethics' for the organization and its members.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page notes ASNE's origins included hammering out a code of ethics (October 1922) as a foundational organizational standard; no detailed provisions are given on this page, but the code is presented as a central governing/ethical standard for members and editorial practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Membership eligibility (original rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: ASNE 'would be an organization of individual editors of big-city papers — limiting membership to editors of newspapers in cities of 100,000 or more.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This was the founders' initial membership criterion; the page also notes 'Since then, rules have been loosened extensively,' indicating eligibility later broadened. Use as an historical criterion for who qualified as a member.

rubrics_metrics.name: Newsroom Employment Census metrics
rubrics_metrics.description: The Diversity Committee was formed to evaluate employee diversity using the Newsroom Employment Census. The census 'queried every daily newspaper and online news site in the United States to determine the number of news staffers as well as their gender and race as part of the organization's yearly census.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This describes specific measurement dimensions used by ASNE to assess newsroom diversity: total number of news staffers, gender composition, and racial composition (collected annually). The census is an evaluative tool for newsroom diversity and staffing levels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sunshine Week principles
rubrics_metrics.description: Sunshine Week is 'an annual event led by ASNE that promotes open government and transparent journalism.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As an initiative, Sunshine Week embodies evaluative/advocacy standards emphasizing government openness and journalistic transparency. It functions as a programmatic criterion for promoting and assessing practices that increase public access to government information and transparent reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: ASNE Awards — categories of journalistic excellence
rubrics_metrics.description: The ASNE Awards included: Batten Medal; Osborn Award for Editorial Leadership; Sulzberger Award for Online Storytelling; Howell Award for Nondeadline Writing; Royko Award for Commentary/Column Writing; Distinguished Writing on Diversity Award; Local Accountability Reporting Award; Community Service Photojournalism Award; Breaking News Writing award; Raymond Clapper Memorial Award.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These award categories imply evaluative dimensions for journalism (editorial leadership, online storytelling, nondeadline feature writing, commentary/columning, writing on diversity, local accountability reporting, community-service-oriented photojournalism, breaking news writing, etc.). The page lists categories but does not provide the detailed judging criteria for each award.

rubrics_metrics.name: Project focus areas: diversity, credibility, readership
rubrics_metrics.description: ASNE 'ran several projects... Projects subject areas have included diversity, credibility and readership.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These topic areas represent programmatic priorities and implicit standards for projects and initiatives ASNE would pursue or evaluate: improving newsroom diversity, enhancing credibility of journalism, and increasing readership. No detailed metrics are given on the page.

rubrics_metrics.name: Educational support standard (my.hsj.org)
rubrics_metrics.description: During the early 2010s, ASNE ran my.hsj.org, which 'acted as a webhosting platform for high school newspapers and featured lessons in journalism, publishing, and advertising.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This indicates a standard of providing practical educational resources and infrastructure for secondary-school journalism (webhosting plus curricular lessons). The page notes the site hosted over 5,000 newspapers before it was shut down in 2013 because 'there are so many more options available to schools.'
